module: Celiac Disease and Small Bowel Enteropathies

steps.say: Start every suspected coeliac workup with the same blood pair, because the antibody result means nothing without knowing the child can make it. Anti tissue transglutaminase IgA is exquisitely sensitive, yet it vanishes falsely in IgA deficiency. So order total serum IgA alongside, while the child still eats gluten freely. A positive tTG on a gluten free diet proves nothing, so never start the diet before testing.
steps.tx: Order **first-line screening serology** as anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA (anti-tTG IgA, the coeliac antibody) together with total serum IgA (the background antibody level) in every suspected case. This pair is the mandatory first investigation while the child eats a normal gluten containing diet, since the antibody fades once gluten is withdrawn. A positive anti-tTG IgA with normal total IgA moves the child toward confirmation, while any negative result on an already restricted diet needs repeating after a proper gluten challenge.

vis.alt: Two-panel coeliac diagram. One side shows gluten, tissue transglutaminase, presentation by HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8, and antibodies to tTG, endomysium, and deamidated gliadin. The other side shows normal villi, villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes, dermatitis herpetitis with granular IgA, and iron or folate malabsorption.
vis.caption: Anti-tTG IgA is the antibody this pathway produces. Total IgA still has to be measured with it, and that pairing is not drawn. Illustration: StewardMD.

steps.say: A small slice of children cannot make IgA at all, and their coeliac screen will lie to you. When total IgA comes back below zero point two, throw away the IgA based tests entirely. Switch to IgG based assays such as deamidated gliadin peptide IgG or tTG IgG, which stay reliable without background IgA. Missing this switch is the commonest reason coeliac disease hides for years in these children.
steps.tx: Apply the **selective IgA deficiency protocol** whenever total IgA is below 0.2 g/L (the deficiency cutoff). In selective IgA deficiency, IgA based tests (tests measuring the IgA antibody class) turn falsely negative, so IgG based tests (tests measuring the IgG antibody class), namely deamidated gliadin peptide IgG or anti-tTG IgG, must be used instead. Recheck levels over time, because partial deficiency can evolve, and refer persistent seronegative but suspicious cases for duodenal biopsy rather than reassurance.

steps.say: Not every positive child needs a camera down the throat anymore. When the antibody titre screams at ten times normal and a second blood sample confirms endomysial positivity, the guidelines let you diagnose without biopsy. The two samples must be separate bleeds, and the family must agree to a lifelong gluten free diet first. Anything less than tenfold, or a wavering EMA, still goes to endoscopy.
steps.tx: Use the **ten-times ULN no-biopsy rule** under ESPGHAN 2020 guidance (the European coeliac guideline). If anti-tTG IgA reaches or exceeds 10 times the upper limit of normal (ULN, the laboratory reference ceiling), a biopsy-free diagnosis is established when endomysial antibodies (EMA-IgA, the confirmatory antibody) test positive on a second, separate blood draw. Counsel the family before testing that a positive result commits the child to lifelong strict gluten exclusion, and biopsy any child who falls short of either condition.

nodes.label: Positive anti-tTG IgA on gluten diet

steps.say: Families often arrive clutching gene reports, so set the record straight early. Carrying DQ2 or DQ8 barely raises risk, while lacking both almost rules coeliac out. That makes the gene test a tool for exclusion, useful in a sibling who hates blood tests or a child already gluten free. Since twenty twenty, it plays no part in confirming the no biopsy pathway, so never delay treatment waiting for it.
steps.tx: Treat **HLA typing obsolete for confirmation** as current doctrine. HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 testing (gene markers for coeliac susceptibility) carries a negative predictive value above 99%, meaning absence of both markers virtually excludes disease, but it is no longer required for the non-biopsy diagnostic pathway under 2020 criteria. Reserve genotyping for exclusion scenarios such as at-risk siblings or children already on a gluten free diet, and never order it to confirm a diagnosis the serology already secures.

steps.say: When biopsy is needed, the pathologist grades destruction in a stepwise ladder you should read fluently. Scattered lymphocytes between surface cells mark the earliest stage, then the crypts stretch downward, and finally the villi themselves flatten in thirds from partial to total. Tropical sprue can mimic that flattened picture, so serology decides between them. Always marry the Marsh grade to the antibody story before labelling the child.
steps.tx: Read the **modified Marsh-Oberhuber classification** on duodenal biopsy histology as Marsh 1 (intraepithelial lymphocytosis above 25/100 enterocytes, excess immune cells among absorptive cells), Marsh 2 (crypt hyperplasia, elongated dividing crypts), and Marsh 3 (villous atrophy graded 3a partial, 3b subtotal, 3c total flattening). Villous blunting also appears in tropical sprue, shown beside normal villi here, so positive coeliac serology separates the two. Grade severity guides prognosis, because Marsh 3c recovers slowest on diet.

vis.alt: Side by side drawings of normal small bowel villi and the shortened villi with crypt changes of tropical sprue.
vis.caption: Tropical sprue mucosa compared with normal villi, showing partial villous atrophy. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Coeliac disease loves company, so hunt it actively in high risk clinics rather than waiting for diarrhoea. Test every newly diagnosed type one diabetic, every child with Down syndrome, and girls with Turner syndrome, plus thyroid and Williams reviews. Most of these children have silent disease picked up only by screening, and catching them early protects growth and bone. Put coeliac serology on their annual checklist without exception.
steps.tx: Screen the **associated conditions and high-risk groups** systematically. Coeliac prevalence climbs in type 1 diabetes (5-10% of diabetic children), Down syndrome (5-12%), Turner syndrome, Williams syndrome, and autoimmune thyroiditis. These children are often asymptomatic (without gut complaints) at detection, presenting instead with short stature, anaemia or delayed puberty. Arrange periodic serological surveillance in each group, because seroconversion (turning antibody positive) can occur years after an initial negative screen.

steps.say: Prescribing a gluten free diet means teaching label arithmetic, not just handing a food list. The safe ceiling sits below ten to twenty parts per million, roughly a crumb, so oats, sauces and shared fryers all need scrutiny. Link every family to a dietitian and a support group at diagnosis. Then monitor growth, iron and vitamin D yearly, because the diet itself can unbalance nutrition when followed blindly.
steps.tx: Hold the **strict gluten-free diet threshold** at under 10-20 parts per million (ppm, milligrams of gluten per kilogram of food) or below 10-20 mg/day of ingested gluten. Wheat, barley and rye go out entirely, while certified gluten free oats are allowed only when tolerated; shared cooking surfaces and fryers need separate utensils. Follow weight, height velocity, haemoglobin, iron, calcium and vitamin D at review, since both ongoing gluten exposure and an unbalanced substitute diet impair growth.

steps.say: Rarely, an infant with undiagnosed coeliac disease crashes with profuse watery diarrhoea, a swollen belly and shocking weakness. Potassium and protein plummet together while the blood turns acidic, and ordinary rehydration fails. Recognise this celiac crisis early, resuscitate aggressively with potassium and albumin, and start systemic steroids promptly. Such infants need intensive care, not a routine diet clinic referral.
steps.tx: Recognise **celiac crisis** as a life-threatening presentation in young infants featuring severe hypokalemia (dangerously low potassium), hypoproteinemia (low blood protein with edema), metabolic acidosis (acidic blood chemistry), and profuse secretory diarrhea unresponsive to standard rehydration. It typically strikes undiagnosed infants after an infectious trigger or abrupt gluten load. Resuscitate with intravenous potassium and albumin, correct acidosis, and give systemic corticosteroids (whole body steroids) early alongside intensive monitoring.
